decisions.quote:
3.1 Actual Sample
Sample was 51 subjects between the ages of 18 and 35, with normal or corrected-to-
normal vision and no history of neurological disorders. Eight subjects were excluded
from final analysis because impedances were too high (>5kΩ) in at least one of the elec-
trodes in which the statistical analyses were to be performed, or because of excessive
muscle artifacts. Thus, the final sample included in the analysis was 43 subjects.
decisions.reason: The primary report ('Replication of “Errors Are Aversive” by Greg Hajcak & Dan Foti (2008, Psychological Science)') is a completed empirical replication that collected new EEG and startle EMG data from 51 new participants (43 analyzed after exclusions) performing the flanker task with auditory startle probes to re-test Hajcak & Foti's (2008) published finding that error-related negativity (ERN) amplitude correlates with error-potentiated startle (EPS) magnitude. The dependent original identity (Hajcak & Foti, 2008, paired with blind target 0) and failed replication outcome (Section 5.1 explicitly concludes 'we consider this to be a failure to replicate but with extremely similar results' because the ERN-EPS correlation r = -.25, p = .11 did not reach significance) are directly confirmed in the primary text. Subsequent exploratory pooled-data and outlier analyses in Section 5.2 do not alter the primary record type of replication.

corrected_value.title: Time Course of Error-Potentiated Startle and its Relationship to Error-Related Brain Activity

decisions.quote:
Importantly, one of the original authors attempted to replicate this correlation result
in a subsequent study (Riesel, Weinberg, Moran, & Hajcak, 2013, Journal of Psychophys-
iology). They found that the correlation between the ERN and EPS was only significant
when assessed in a subgroup of participants who showed large ERNs (via a median split
based on ERN amplitude). Therefore, we attempted this same analysis strategy and per-
formed a median split based on ERN amplitude and re-assessed the correlation between
ERN and EPS magnitude in this subgroup of participants (see Figure 4). Consistent with
the Riesel et al. (2013) study, we found a significant correlation between ERN and EPS
in this subgroup of participants (r = -.63, p < .01).
decisions.reason: Parent independently verified0046original publisher-typeset nine-page primary report with exact title, four authors,2013issue27(2):51–59 and printedDOI10.1027/0269-8803/a000093. Current Section5.2 explicitly repeats that original high-ERN median-split correlation analysis in new participants, distinct from shipped1895Hajcak/Foti2008whole-sample finding. The earlier missing-title obstruction is resolved by new primary identity proof, without altering the blind coding or assigning an unrequested subgroup outcome. The DOI stays in provenance because the current text does not print it. PrimaryPDFcontrol-character signs remain untouched.
